title: SSD & Flash Internals
summary: Why flash memory can't simply overwrite a page in place, and what that one constraint does to every write an SSD performs.

slides.markdown:
An SSD stores bits in **NAND flash cells** — each cell traps electric charge on an isolated floating gate, and the presence or absence (or level) of that charge is read as data. There's no moving arm, no spinning platter: the entire mechanism is electrical, which is why SSDs have no mechanical latency wall to hit ([hdd-mechanics-and-performance](hdd-mechanics-and-performance)).

That charge persists without power, which is what makes flash **non-volatile**. But trapping and releasing charge isn't symmetric — and that asymmetry is the root of nearly every quirky behavior SSDs have that HDDs don't.

Flash is organized in two granularities that don't match: **reads and writes** happen at **page** granularity (commonly 4–16KB), but **erases** happen at **block** granularity — a block holds many pages (often 128–256 of them).

This mismatch is the single most important fact about flash: you can write a fresh page cheaply, but you can only reset a page back to a writable state by erasing the **entire block** it lives in, taking every other page in that block along with it.

slides.sectionTitle: Why you can't overwrite in place
slides.markdown:
Writing a flash cell only works in one direction: the write operation can pull charge **into** a cell (setting bits toward `0`) but cannot selectively push it back out of just one cell. Clearing charge — resetting a cell to its erased `1` state — requires a much higher voltage applied to the **whole block** at once.

So to change a single bit that's already been written, the SSD can't just "overwrite" it: the containing block must first be erased entirely, and then rewritten. This is the direct cause of the page/block mismatch's real-world cost.

Seeing the pages packed into one block clarifies why a single-page update can't be cheap: the whole block has to be erased before any of its pages can be written again.

![A flash block containing many pages, illustrating that the whole block must be erased before any page inside it can be rewritten](assets/flash-block-erase.svg)

This is why SSD controllers never erase-then-write in place for a small update — they write the new data to a **fresh**, already-erased page elsewhere, and deal with reclaiming the stale one later ([ssd-controller-management](ssd-controller-management)).

assets.alt: A flash block containing many pages, illustrating that the whole block must be erased before any page inside it can be rewritten

slides.markdown:
SSDs are fast at **random reads** because reading a page has no mechanical cost at all — any page can be reached in roughly the same tiny time, unlike an HDD where random reads mean physically moving a head.

Writes are a different story. Because in-place overwrite is impossible, every write the SSD receives really means: find (or make) an already-erased page, write there, mark the old page stale, and eventually reclaim it. That extra bookkeeping — invisible to the application issuing the write — is why SSD write behavior is genuinely more involved than it looks from the outside.

Flash cells can store more than one bit by distinguishing finer levels of trapped charge — but more bits per cell costs endurance and speed.

| Type | Bits/cell | Endurance | Relative cost/GB |
|---|---|---|---|
| SLC | 1 | Highest (~50k–100k writes) | Highest |
| MLC | 2 | Medium (~3k–10k writes) | Medium |
| TLC | 3 | Lower (~1k–3k writes) | Lower |
| QLC | 4 | Lowest (~100s–1k writes) | Lowest |

More bits per cell packs more capacity into the same silicon, which is why consumer SSDs are overwhelmingly TLC/QLC today — the endurance trade-off matters far less for typical read-heavy consumer workloads than the cost-per-gigabyte win.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: how endurance turns into a lifespan
slides.subTitle: P/E cycles, drive writes per day, and warranty numbers
slides.markdown:
A TLC SSD rated for 3,000 program/erase (P/E) cycles per cell, 1TB capacity, and a workload writing 50GB/day:

```
total writeable capacity over life = 1000GB * 3000 cycles = 3,000,000 GB written
years of endurance = 3,000,000 GB / 50 GB/day / 365 days ~= 164 years
```

That number looks enormous because it assumes every write is perfectly spread across every cell (ideal wear leveling) and ignores **write amplification** — the controller often writes more physical bytes than the host requested ([SSD Controller & Management](ssd-controller-management)). A workload with heavy write amplification (say 5x) effectively divides that lifespan by 5, down to roughly 33 years — still comfortable for a consumer drive, but this is exactly the calculation datacenter procurement teams run before choosing SLC/MLC/TLC for a given write-heavy workload, where the numbers get much tighter.

slides.sectionTitle: Why flash needs error correction, not just clean reads
slides.subTitle: Read disturb, retention, and voltage-threshold drift
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Reading flash is a purely non-destructive electrical operation, so repeated reads are free and safe."

**Why it's wrong:** reading a page applies a voltage to neighboring cells in the same block, and repeated reads of one page can gradually shift the charge level in *nearby* cells — a phenomenon called **read disturb**. Separately, stored charge slowly leaks over time even with zero access (**retention loss**), which is worse on cheaper, denser cells (TLC/QLC) than SLC. Both effects mean a bit that was written correctly can later be read back wrong. This is exactly why every SSD controller runs strong **ECC (error-correcting code)** on every page, and why the drive proactively re-writes ('refreshes') data that's been sitting unread for a long time or read too many times — flash reliability is a controller-managed property, not a property of the raw cells alone.

slides.subTitle: Stacking cells vertically instead of shrinking them further
slides.markdown:
For years, flash density grew by shrinking each cell (planar scaling) — but at a small enough size, cells sit close enough that their charge interferes with neighbors, hurting endurance and reliability. **3D NAND** sidesteps this by stacking many layers of cells **vertically** on the same silicon footprint, rather than shrinking them further in the horizontal plane.

This is why modern SSD spec sheets advertise a layer count (96-layer, 176-layer, 232-layer, and climbing) rather than a shrinking process node the way CPUs do — vertical stacking, not horizontal shrinking, is now the main lever for adding capacity without sacrificing per-cell reliability. It's a direct hardware answer to the endurance/density trade-off from the previous slide: more capacity without cramming cells closer together.
